question: The breath that calms you down

say: You keep telling yourself to calm down while you're breathing like something is chasing you.
Your body has a better way.
Your body was built with a brake you can reach: when you breathe in, your heart speeds up a little, and when you breathe out, it slows down.
Your body already sighs every few minutes without you noticing, taking a second breath to reopen tiny air sacs in your lungs.
So sigh on purpose: breathe in twice, then let one long, slow breath out.

In a Stanford study of mostly students, five minutes a day of this for a month lifted mood more than meditation did, and across twelve trials, breathing exercises cut stress by a small to medium amount.
It's a useful tool, not a magic one.
Do it for five minutes a day, and skip hard, fast breathing drills, because they can make you dizzy.
And never practise breathing drills or breath-holding in or near water.
If stress is getting too much to cope with, or nothing you try is helping, talk to a doctor.
If you or someone you know needs help right now, or you've seriously harmed yourself, call emergency services.
Let's get you back to factory settings.

lehrer2014: Lehrer PM, Gevirtz R. Heart rate variability biofeedback: how and why does it work? Front Psychol 2014;5:756: "RSA is the heart pattern that occurs when heart rate increases during inhalation and decreases during exhalation."
balban2023: Balban MY et al. Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal. Cell Rep Med 2023;4(1):100895: remote randomised trial, 108 participants (mostly Stanford undergraduates), 5 min a day for a month; cyclic sighing raised positive affect significantly more than mindfulness meditation; no differences in state anxiety or negative affect between groups; no non-practice control; "Inhales increase heart rate and exhales decrease heart rate via respiratory sinus arrhythmia"
li2016: Li P et al. The peptidergic control circuit for sighing. Nature 2016;530:293-297: "Sighs also occur spontaneously every few minutes to reinflate alveoli"
severs2022: Severs LJ, Vlemincx E, Ramirez JM. The psychophysiology of the sigh: I. Biol Psychol 2022;170:108313: sighs "play a critical role in controlling lung compliance by preventing the collapse of alveoli"
ucla2016: UCLA Health news release, 8 Feb 2016, Jack Feldman: "It starts out as a normal breath, but before you exhale, you take a second breath on top of it." (press release)
fincham2023: Fincham GW et al. Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: a meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials. Sci Rep 2023;13:432: 12 RCTs, 785 adults; self-reported stress g = -0.35 (95% CI -0.55 to -0.14), "small-to-medium"; the authors warn against "a miscalibration between hype and evidence"
medlinehv: MedlinePlus, Hyperventilation: "Excessive breathing creates a low level of carbon dioxide in your blood. This causes many of the symptoms of hyperventilation", including "Feeling lightheaded, dizzy"
cdc2015: Boyd C et al. Fatal and nonfatal drowning outcomes related to dangerous underwater breath-holding behaviors, New York State, 1988-2011. MMWR 2015;64(19): hyperventilation or breath-holding before swimming can cause loss of consciousness underwater
nhsstress: NHS, Stress (reviewed 6 Mar 2026): "See a GP if: you’re struggling to cope with stress; things you’re trying yourself are not helping"; "Call 999 or go to A&E now if: you or someone you know needs immediate help; you have seriously harmed yourself, for example by taking a drug overdose"
nhsbreath: NHS, Breathing exercises for stress (reviewed 12 Jun 2026): breathe in through the nose and out through the mouth, counting 1 to 5 each way; "Repeat for at least 5 minutes"; "most benefit if you do it regularly, as part of your daily routine"
